analysis.one_liner: Expands the overtime-pay exemption to cover more computer professionals.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote — it was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and died there, leaving overtime protections for network and database workers in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Labor Standards Act requires employers to pay at least the minimum wage and time-and-a-half for overtime, but it exempts certain skilled computer employees. This bill would rewrite that exemption to add computer network and database analysts, plus systems, network, and database designers and developers, and would define 'network' to include the Internet, intranets, and the web [S2] [S3]. Workers swept into the exemption would no longer be legally entitled to overtime pay. The bill was introduced in October 1999 and referred to committee, which never acted on it [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers of computer professionals — software companies, IT departments, and tech service firms — gain a larger workforce they can require to work long hours without paying overtime, and they gain certainty that job titles like network analyst and database designer are exempt [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Rewrites the FLSA computer-professional exemption to cover computer systems, network, and database analysts, designers, and developers — not just programmers and software engineers — so those workers lose the right to overtime pay [S2] [S3].
Defines 'network' to include the Internet, intranets, and the world wide web, bringing web-era job titles squarely inside the exemption [S3].
Declares exempt workers to be 'employees in a professional capacity,' a category that signals to employers these workers are outside minimum-wage and overtime protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Computer network and database analysts, and systems, network, and database designers and developers, who would lose their legal right to overtime pay (and, in edge cases, minimum-wage coverage) for hours worked beyond 40 a week [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Network and database analysts and developers

drawbacks.text: The core cost falls on workers: analysts, designers, and developers newly covered by the exemption could be required to work long hours with no overtime premium, shifting income from employees to employers [S2] [S3].

The bill anchors the hourly pay threshold for exempt workers to the rate set by a 1996 law rather than to a current or automatically updated figure, so the cutoff would not rise with wages or inflation [S3].

A good-faith case for the bill existed: the existing exemption named only programmers and software engineers, and employers argued that similarly skilled analysts and developers were stuck in a gray zone that invited misclassification lawsuits. The bill would have settled that by exempting them — but it settled it in the employer's favor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered employers legal certainty and lower labor costs for a growing class of technology jobs, but its main effect was to take overtime pay away from skilled workers whose jobs did not fit the old exemption's job titles. For the workers affected, the trade was a one-way loss; the 'clarification' cut only one direction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee in October 1999, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews (D-NJ) introduced the bill on October 7, 1999, joined by Rep. Graham (R) and Rep. Owens (D) [S1] [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S5].
No further action was taken — no markup, no floor vote, no Senate companion action appears in the record — and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Computer workers kept their overtime protections. Employers who would have gained a broader exemption from paying overtime did not get it.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to broaden the computer-professional overtime exemption.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Held the referred bill without scheduling a markup or any further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny: a Democratic sponsor with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, and no votes were ever taken on the bill [S1] [S4].

industries.note: The industry wanted a broader overtime exemption so analysts, designers, and developers could work long hours without premium pay; because the bill died, employers must keep paying overtime to workers who don't fit the old exemption. The industry's gain under the bill would have come directly out of workers' paychecks.
